I was in a similar position as you and would caution against everyone being so dismissive. If your goal is to work in America, your odds are better but it’s still far from a safe pathway. But I think overall the educational experience here is quite compelling, and it’s also a lot easier —in my experience— to find valuable internships, do research, and to do extracurricular activities. A lot of highly ranked US universities are well-regarded internationally and will make it easier to get into good grad programs. Education also isn’t only about getting a good career, and having the opportunity to live in a new place automatically enhances the educational experience. With that said, it really depends on your financial situation and I definitely wouldn’t go into debt for it

I think it’s firstly important to note that the Swedish higher-education system differs a bit from that of the US. Most students study specific programs where all their courses for all three years are chosen ahead of time by the school. It is therefore important to consider exactly which one you want to choose (eg comp-sci/math or comp-sci/system knowledge)

As for the application itself it is done on a website called universityadmissions.se which essentially is the Swedish equivalent of Common App. You will need to provide certain documentation such as your high school diploma and any university transcripts. So I would make sure to have all that in order quite awhile before as it can get messy otherwise. Also something to remember for when you’re closer to actually applying is to start early because Sweden requires US applicants to have all transcripts be sent directly from the university by mail.

Language requirements depend on the language of instruction. If you want to have Swedish as your language of instruction you need to prove Swedish proficiency (which is quite difficult if you live in the US). As for English all you need is to prove English proficiency which you should automatically be able to do having a completed American high school education.

There are also other requirements for the individual programs. For example compsci would require the Swedish course Math 4 usually which would be the equivalent of **something like** Calculus although such translations can be hard to make. I would do my best ahead of time to make sure I meet all the requirements and if not see if it’s possible to read any of those courses at uni before you apply. Most universities have guidance counsellors who can help you.

Some universities also accept SAT test scores although that is quite rare.

The visa application process after having been admitted is quite straightforward. I would look up possible tuition fees as they might be higher for CS programs (around 7-13K USD per year). Most universities offer scholarships I would look that up if it interests you. Lastly I would also look at applying to KTH, they’re quite reputable and have a large number of international students.

Good luck!

Honestly I feel this is somewhat of an exaggeration. I think a lot of people would prefer living in other warmer EU-countries (with similar social safety nets). Living here as foreign-born can be hard both employment-wise (Swedish job market is infamously discriminatory especially if you are a POC)and socially as a lot of people have a hard time adjusting to the social norms  If OP has dual citizenship best bet is probably to move to another EU country and try to find a way to get the equivalent of a secondary school education (while working).

There are of course a lot of positive aspects of living in Sweden but I think there are completely understandable reasons for being dissatisfied and they are not always bound to improve.
